opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and it gets at something I think is a big inefficiency in how most organizations do machine learning today.

Most of the world's valuable enterprise data lives in relational databases: customers, transactions, products, orders, support tickets, all spread across many tables linked by primary and foreign keys. But our machine learning models want a single flat table, one row per entity and a fixed set of columns. So the standard workflow is that a data scientist sits down and manually turns this rich multi-table structure into a flat feature vector. They write SQL joins and aggregations: number of purchases in the last 30 days, average order value, time since last login, and so on.

That process has a few fundamental problems.

First, it's extremely labor-intensive. Feature engineering often takes most of the time in a predictive modeling project, and it has to be largely redone for every new task. Churn prediction, fraud detection, and recommendations each get their own pipeline, even though they sit on top of the same database.

Second, it loses information. Every time you aggregate, you're compressing. You decide upfront that "count of purchases in the last 30 days" is what matters, and you throw away the sequence, the timing, the specific products, and the multi-hop relationships. For example, the users who bought the same items as this user, and what those users did next. Humans just can't enumerate all the useful combinations of joins and aggregations across many tables.

Third, it's brittle and hard to maintain. These pipelines are tied to specific schemas and assumptions, and when the data or business changes, things break or quietly degrade.

The key insight behind relational deep learning is that a relational database is really a graph. Each row is a node, each table is a node type, and foreign-key relationships are edges. Once you see it that way, you can apply graph neural networks directly to the raw database. Message passing over that graph essentially learns the joins and aggregations for you, end to end, optimized for the prediction task you care about. And because these databases evolve over time, you have to treat time carefully: you only let the model see information available before the prediction time, so you don't leak the future into training.

What we've seen, including in the benchmarking work we did with RelBench, is that this approach can match or beat carefully hand-engineered pipelines built by experienced data scientists, while taking a fraction of the human effort. You go from weeks of feature work to defining the task and training a model.

And the bigger picture is that this sets us up for foundation models over relational data. Just as we moved away from hand-crafted features in computer vision and NLP once we had models that learn representations directly from pixels and text, I think structured enterprise data is going through that same transition now. The raw database becomes the input, and the model learns what matters.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes manual feature engineering as labor-intensive and brittle, but does not compare it to relying on car expertise to handcraft car-detection features.

r002.rationale: It says manual aggregation compresses information and reflects choices made upfront, but does not clearly characterize the resulting summaries as shaped by human biases.

r003.rationale: The response says relational models learn joins and aggregations and can match or beat engineered pipelines, but does not clearly explain that they discover more predictive signal than those features capture.

r004.rationale: The response does not discuss linear models or state that neural networks offer no predictive advantage when the underlying relationship is linear.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is, if you look at how machine learning is actually done on top of relational databases today, it's really a very manual, very artisanal process. You have an enterprise with, say, dozens or hundreds of tables, and a data scientist wants to predict something, maybe customer churn, or whether a transaction is fraudulent, or what a user is going to buy next. What do they do? They sit down and they start writing SQL. They join tables together, they aggregate, they compute things like "how many purchases did this customer make in the last thirty days," "what was the average order value," "how long since their last login," and so on. And they do this over and over until they've flattened all that rich relational structure into a single table, a feature matrix, that they can then feed into something like XGBoost.

And this works, right? It's been the state of the art for twenty years. But there are a couple of problems with it. First, it's incredibly slow and expensive. It's weeks or months of human effort per prediction task, and the person doing it has to be both a domain expert and a data engineering expert. Second, and I think this is the deeper issue, it's fundamentally lossy. Every time you aggregate, you're throwing information away. You're making a bet about which signals matter, and you're compressing a whole sequence of events into a handful of summary statistics. And the features you end up with are limited by human imagination. Nobody is going to hand-write the three-hop feature that says "this customer bought products that were frequently purchased by users who later churned." But that signal might be in the data.

So the insight behind relational deep learning is actually quite simple once you see it. A relational database is a graph. Every row is a node, every foreign key is an edge connecting rows across tables. The schema tells you the node types and edge types. So instead of manually collapsing that graph into a table, you keep it as a graph and you let a graph neural network learn directly on top of it. The model does message passing across the foreign-key relationships, it learns its own representations of what matters, and crucially, it learns them end to end for the specific prediction task. The feature engineering is no longer a human step. It's part of the model.

And what I find exciting is that this mirrors what happened in computer vision and in NLP. We used to hand-design SIFT features for images, we used to hand-design n-grams and parsers for text, and in both cases deep learning that works on the raw representation ended up winning, not because the human features were bad, but because learned representations scale and generalize in a way that handcrafted ones don't. I think relational data, which honestly is where most of the world's valuable data actually lives, is the next domain where that transition is going to happen. We just hadn't had the right abstraction for it, and I think treating the database as a graph is that abstraction.

r001.rationale: The response says manual feature work requires domain and data engineering expertise, but it does not compare that reliance to expertise about cars or handcrafted car-detection features.

r002.rationale: It describes aggregation as compressing data into summary statistics, shaped by human choices about which signals matter and limited by human imagination.

r003.rationale: It explains that graph neural networks learn directly across relational links and can capture signals, such as multi-hop patterns, that manual features may miss.

r004.rationale: The response does not state that a neural network offers no predictive advantage over a linear model when the underlying relationship is linear.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that the relationships in a database contain a lot of predictive information, but getting that information into a traditional machine learning model requires a lot of manual work. You have to decide which tables to join, what to aggregate, and over what time windows. Those choices become your features, and you repeat that process for each prediction task.

Relational deep learning lets us learn from that structure directly. We represent rows as nodes and the relationships between rows as edges. Then the model can follow those connections and learn which information is useful for a particular prediction.

Think about predicting whether a customer will purchase again. You have information about that customer, their previous purchases, the products they bought, and other customers who bought those products. Instead of manually compressing all of that into a fixed set of features, we let the model learn how to combine it.

So the appeal is both reducing the feature engineering effort and making better use of the information already in the database. You still have to define the prediction task carefully and ensure you only use information available at prediction time. But you shift much of the work from hand-designing features to learning representations.

r002.rationale: It describes manually chosen features as fixed and task-specific, but does not characterize them as summaries shaped by human biases.

r003.rationale: It says relational deep learning can learn which information to use and make better use of database information, but does not clearly state that it discovers more predictive signal than manual features capture.

r004.rationale: The response makes no claim about neural networks versus linear models when the underlying relationship is linear.

sol-6.1.text:
The key reason is that the relationships in a database contain a lot of predictive information. With manual feature engineering, you have to decide which tables to join, which relationships to follow, and how to aggregate the results. Those decisions take substantial effort, and you often have to revisit them for every prediction task.

Relational deep learning lets us learn from that structure directly. We represent rows as nodes and the relationships between them as edges, then learn how to combine information across related records. Instead of committing in advance to a particular set of aggregations, we can learn representations that are useful for the prediction we want to make.

That doesn’t mean domain knowledge stops mattering. But it shifts the work from handcrafting every feature toward defining the task, getting the data right, and making sure the model uses only information available at prediction time.
